passage:
Week one. Amandeep took his son Jatin's phone at nine every night and banned the Friday football group outright. Jatin said nothing, just shut his door hard. Three days later Amandeep found a second phone, an old one, charging behind the books.
Week two. Amandeep sat on Jatin's bed instead of shouting. "I was scared about the late walks home. That's the real reason." Jatin stared at the floor, then muttered, "You could've just said that."
Week four. They had worked it out together: football on Fridays, home by eight, phone out of the room at ten, and Jatin picks which weekend night runs late. On Friday a text arrived, unasked: "Leaving now 👍" Amandeep read it twice and smiled.

qa.q: What did Amandeep find charging behind the books?
qa.a: Amandeep found a second phone, an old one, charging behind the books.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he shut his door hard in week one?
qa.a: He felt controlled and angry at a ban with no reason given, and the hidden phone shows he wanted to keep some freedom, even in secret.

qa.q: Which change in Amandeep's approach made the difference?
qa.a: He shared his real fear, then worked out limits together with Jatin and let him choose within them, which rebuilt trust.

qa.q: How does Amandeep feel when Jatin texts "Leaving now" without being asked?
qa.a: Relieved and touched 😊; the secrecy has turned into Jatin keeping him in the loop by choice.

grounding: It shows a father seeing strict rules produce secrecy and then shifting to explaining reasons, offering choices within limits and staying connected.

passage:
Shreya, you think your papa was always this calm? When he was fifteen, your Thatha ran this house like a police station. No friends after school, no cinema, radio off at eight. And your papa, such a sweet boy, started lying. He'd say he was at tuition and be at the cricket ground. Once he came home with a split lip and wouldn't say how.
Your Thatha was furious at first. Then one night I heard him on the verandah, talking to your papa quietly. "I made these rules because I'm afraid for you. Tell me which ones feel unfair." They sat there till midnight. After that it was cricket three evenings a week, home before dark, and Thatha even went to watch some matches.
The lies stopped. Not all at once, but they stopped.

qa.q: Where was Shreya's papa when he said he was at tuition?
qa.a: He was at the cricket ground.

qa.q: Why do you think Shreya's papa started lying at fifteen?
qa.a: The rules were so tight, with no friends, no cinema and the radio off at eight, that he felt he had no room of his own; hiding seemed the only way to get some freedom.

qa.q: What did Thatha do that helped end the lies?
qa.a: He explained his fear honestly, asked which rules felt unfair, and agreed on limits together, even going to watch some matches to stay close.

qa.q: How might Shreya see papa differently after hearing this story?
qa.a: Shreya might realise papa knows from experience how harsh rules push teenagers into secrets, which may explain the calm way he parents now.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a father who saw strict rules breed secrecy and changed to explaining reasons, giving choices within limits and staying close.

passage:
Sahil worked night shifts at a call centre, so his rules for Keerthana came by text: no going out, no phone after ten, no friends over. For a month she agreed to everything. Then her class teacher called to say Keerthana had missed two afternoons of school.
He wanted to take her phone away for a year. Instead, on his one free morning, with the water tanker blaring outside and an hour left before he had to sleep, he sat across from her with two cups of tea. "I made all those rules because I'm never here to see you. That's my worry, not your fault. Where were you?"
She had been at a friend's house, practising for a dance competition he'd said no to. They settled it before the tanker left: practice twice a week at the friend's house, with a call when she arrives.

qa.q: Why had Keerthana missed two afternoons of school?
qa.a: She had been at a friend's house, practising for a dance competition.

qa.q: What does Sahil's first urge to take her phone for a year suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt angry and deceived after the teacher's call and wanted even stricter control.

qa.q: What did Sahil do in that short hour that worked?
qa.a: He admitted the rules came from his own worry, asked instead of accusing, and agreed on practice twice a week with a call on arrival, a choice within clear limits.

qa.q: What is it like for Keerthana when her father sits down with tea instead of shouting?
qa.a: She likely feels safe enough to tell the truth about the dance practice, because he takes the blame for his worry instead of making her the problem.

grounding: It shows a father noticing his strict rules led to secrecy and moving to reasons, choices within limits and connection despite little time.

passage:
In their Lajpat Nagar flat, Harish had a rule for every hour of fifteen-year-old Parul's day: home by six, no friends' houses, phone on the dining table after nine. By March he noticed things. Her messages were always deleted. She said she'd been at the library when a neighbour had seen her at the park. Once she slammed her door and didn't speak to him for two days.
One night Harish sat on the step outside her room. "I've been making rules without telling you why. Here's why: the main road is dark after seven, and I get scared. Can we choose together? Park with friends till seven, and you text me when you leave."
Parul opened the door a crack. "And the phone?"
"Your call, after ten."
The next evening she texted him from the park gate at five to seven: "Coming home. Want samosas?"

qa.q: What did a neighbour see that didn't match Parul's story?
qa.a: A neighbour had seen her at the park when she said she'd been at the library.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about Parul's secrecy, and what shows it?
qa.a: Harish felt scared for Parul and wanted to reconnect, which is why he sat on the step outside her room and admitted the dark main road frightens him.

qa.q: Which change in Harish's approach turned things around, and why?
qa.a: He explained the real reason for his worry and offered choices within limits, so Parul had room to decide and no need to hide.

qa.q: How might Parul have experienced her father's rules before that night?
qa.a: They probably felt like a cage with no reasons, so hiding and lying seemed the only way to have any life of her own.

grounding: A father sees his strict rules breed secrecy and defiance, then explains his reasons, offers choices within limits and reconnects.

passage:
"Kishore, sit. I'm not going to shout."
"That's new."
"Fair." Ujjwal pulled a chair close. "Last month I banned your late cricket evenings on the ground. Since then you've lied twice about where you were. Your mother found your kit in Faisal's car."
"Because you never listen, Papa. You just say no."
"You're right. I said no without reasons. Here's the reason: the ground has no lights and the road back is a highway. I lie awake."
Kishore looked up.
"So, choices. Weekend games, any time till dark. Or weekday games if someone's parent drives both ways. You pick."
"...Weekends. And Faisal's dad can drive sometimes."
"Deal. And tell me the score after. I actually want to know."
"You hate cricket."
"I like you."

qa.q: Where did Kishore's mother find the cricket kit?
qa.a: In Faisal's car.

qa.q: Why did Kishore answer "That's new" when Ujjwal said he wouldn't shout?
qa.a: Kishore expected another telling-off and felt guarded and a bit bitter, because past talks had only brought bans.

qa.q: Which choice did Ujjwal offer, and why did it work better than the ban?
qa.a: He let Kishore pick between weekend games till dark or weekday games with a parent driving, which kept the safety limit while giving Kishore a real say.

qa.q: How had the ban felt from Kishore's side?
qa.a: To Kishore it felt like being refused without being heard, so lying seemed easier than talking.

grounding: A father notices his ban led to lies, and shifts to giving reasons, offering choices within limits and showing interest.
